column2: What change marks each step from primary to secondary to tertiary chorionic villi?
column3: Primary villi are cytotrophoblast columns within syncytiotrophoblast; extraembryonic mesoderm entering the core makes secondary villi; fetal capillaries developing in the core make tertiary villi.

column2: What distinguishes anchoring villi from floating terminal villi?
column3: Anchoring villi attach the chorionic plate to maternal decidua through cytotrophoblastic columns, while floating terminal villi provide most of the exchange surface.

column2: Why does placental exchange become more efficient as pregnancy advances?
column3: The barrier thins: cytotrophoblast becomes discontinuous, syncytiotrophoblast thins, and fetal capillaries approach the surface, shortening diffusion distance.

column2: How do glucose, amino acids and immunoglobulin G cross the placenta differently from gases?
column3: Gases diffuse, whereas glucose uses facilitated transport, amino acids use active or carrier-mediated transport, and immunoglobulin G crosses by receptor-mediated transcytosis.

column2: Why does spiral artery remodelling matter, and what follows when it is incomplete?
column3: Extravillous trophoblast converts narrow muscular responsive arteries into wide low-resistance channels that sustain high-volume flow; incomplete remodelling is associated with hypoperfusion, fetal growth restriction and pre-eclampsia.

column2: Why is oxygen delivery to the fetus less than uterine oxygen uptake?
column3: The placenta itself consumes oxygen and nutrients, so only part of what the uterus takes up reaches the fetus.

column3: The fetal adrenal and liver provide the precursors that the placenta uses to make oestriol.

column2: What is the purpose of maternal insulin resistance in later pregnancy, and when does it become harmful?
column3: Insulin resistance and increased lipolysis preserve glucose and fuels for the fetus, but excessive dysregulation contributes to gestational diabetes and abnormal growth.

column2: Why is pregnancy not a state of global immunosuppression?
column3: Tolerance relies on local features: syncytiotrophoblast lacks some polymorphic histocompatibility molecules, extravillous trophoblast interacts with uterine natural-killer cells and macrophages, and decidual immune cells regulate remodelling, defence and tolerance.

column2: How does the human placenta become discoid?
column3: Villi persist over the decidua basalis as chorion frondosum and regress elsewhere as chorion laeve, so exchange tissue is confined to one disc.

column3: Amniotic fluid normally permits movement, symmetrical growth and protection from compression; when it is severely reduced early, those supports are lost.

column3: High pulmonary resistance diverts it through the ductus arteriosus to the descending aorta; at birth lung expansion lowers pulmonary resistance, and higher oxygen with reduced prostaglandins constricts the ductus.

column3: A shared placenta has vascular connections between the twins, creating risks such as twin-to-twin transfusion, selective growth restriction and consequences when one twin dies.

column2: Why can the same teratogenic exposure cause loss, malformation or no detectable effect?
column3: Outcome depends on dose, timing, duration, route, maternal metabolism, placental transfer and embryonic genotype, and vulnerability shifts with stage, weeks three to eight carrying high susceptibility to structural malformation.
